beats.role_note: What it will be, in one sentence; the GDD's next milestone (Development Scope) and its version.
beats.narration_text: What I'll build is the next milestone from my game design document, version zero point three, from October seventeenth. In one sentence: a playable Mac build where one run becomes one delivery. A post office menu, one contract across the market, the Lantern Gate at the end, and a second courier, the Engineer, who places turrets.

show.event: four parts of the slice appear in turn

remotion.note: no Remotion render; the board is drawn by tools/build_media.py

props.excerpt: The course version should first polish the existing three-minute loop: clearer enemy readability, stronger integration of the Lantern Gate, Supply Stack, and Lamp-oil Shrine, and continued balance testing. The next playable milestone should add the post-office hub, a simple contract and difficulty selector, persistent destination improvements, and one additional courier: an engineer who places automatic turrets.

beats.role_note: Why anyone would care: the run goes somewhere, and the change persists (PX-03; final's saved data).
beats.narration_text: Why would anyone care? Because the run goes somewhere. When a delivery succeeds, the destination changes, and it's still changed the next time you play, even after a restart. My design doc calls this a visible consequence.

beats.role_note: Comparable games Bao has played (card answer, 23 November 2026) and the one specific difference.
beats.narration_text: I've played Vampire Survivors, Brotato, Twenty Minutes Till Dawn and Halls of Torment. In Vampire Survivors, a run's goal is to outlast the clock. In Brotato, it's to outlast twenty waves. Lanternfall gives a player who likes short runs a destination, and a place that remembers they got there.

beats.role_note: The Engineer: roster rule and trade-off from the GDD; the turret state machine as the planned A9 technique.
beats.narration_text: The second courier is the Engineer. My roster rule gives every courier one advantage, one rule change and one weakness. The Engineer's turret holds an area, at the cost of lower damage and speed. The turret will run on its own state machine: idle, track, fire, cool down. That's my plan for the game AI technique in Assignment nine.

beats.role_note: Who opens it: target role, reader, the first sixty seconds; the stack and export target.
beats.narration_text: Who opens it? I'm aiming at gameplay programmer jobs, so the reader is a hiring manager or a lead gameplay engineer. In the first minute, they open the Mac build, land on the post office menu with keyboard focus already set, read the keys on that screen, press Enter, and they're moving. No manual. Then the lead runs one test command from the readme. It's Godot four point seven point two, Compatibility renderer, exported for macOS.

show.event: constructed storyboard of the first sixty seconds

beats.role_note: What it proves: course skills with existing evidence (tags a5, a6, a7) and what it cannot prove.
beats.narration_text: What does it prove? That I can add new systems to a working game and pin each one with tests a stranger can rerun. The course skills already have evidence: hand-written shaders at tag A-five, particle effects with a cost report at tag A-six, and animation driven by state at tag A-seven, where twenty-three headless runs pass from a fresh clone, and eight of eight mutations are caught. What it can't prove is that the game is fun.

beats.role_note: In and out, with the GDD's R-01 mitigation as the reason for the cut.
beats.narration_text: What's in: the delivery, the post office menu, one contract, the Engineer, one saved record, the lit gate, and a Mac export. What's out, on purpose: the other four couriers, a difficulty selector, more maps, the fog boss, multiplayer, web and mobile. My own risk table says it: one screen, one contract and the Engineer, before anything else.

beats.role_note: The first playable piece (F-04), Bao's answer to Q-01 for this slice, and how anyone would know it ran.
beats.narration_text: First comes the delivery objective, on the route that already exists. My doc left open how a delivery ends. For this slice: survive until the fog lifts, then reach the gate. You'll know it ran when a headless test with a fixed seed drives a run to delivered, and the result panel says so on screen.

beats.role_note: The concrete risk (GDD R-03) against measured A6 cost evidence; the mitigation.
beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Turrets. Every turret hit can spawn the sparks I built in Assignment six, in the busiest minute of the run. And on my Mac, Godot reports zero milliseconds of GPU time under the Compatibility renderer, so I can't read that cost there. So I'll cap the turrets, reuse their shots, measure CPU frame time at the peak wave the way my Assignment six cost test did, use the Vulkan proxy for the GPU, and cut turret sparks first.

remotion.note: no Remotion render; the board is drawn by tools/build_media.py

props.excerpt: | R-03 | Turrets create pathing clutter or excessive runtime cost. | Limit active turrets, reuse objects, and test readability and frame time under maximum enemy load. |

beats.role_note: Why this project: Bao's answers (23 November 2026) on new versus existing skills, with evidence.
beats.narration_text: Why this project? Both reasons: learning, and showing what I have. New to me in this course: Godot and GDScript, shaders and materials, and particles. Animation, state machines and testing, I already had, and tag A-seven is my evidence. The delivery, the save and the turret will be new code in this game.

beats.role_note: Exists versus will exist, by the GDD's own status convention.
beats.narration_text: To be exact about what's real: everything on the left exists, with a tag you can check out. Nothing on the right exists yet, and there's no export yet either. The finished slice is due on December twentieth, tagged A-ten.
